new_statements.rule_in_words: Bikya (Bikyak) is reported as a tone language with three level tones High, Mid, Low, a possible fourth Very Low level, and a Falling contour tone (Kießling's 2007 field analysis, personal communication to Blench). Nothing is said about stress or accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: not mentioned (no stress/accent statement anywhere in the article; the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur)
new_statements.exceptions: The Very Low tone is flagged as uncertain '(?VL)'. Blench adds general caveats: 'The data on Furu is too uncertain to be sure it has been correctly classified' (p. 12) and, for the vowel count, fn. 14 'From the fragmentary data it is unclear if the vowels are phonetic or phonemic'.
new_statements.identity_note: Row label 'Furu / Bikyak', reference 'Kießling (p.c.)': Bikyak is Kießling's and ELAR's spelling of Bikya (byb), the Furu-cluster language of Furubana that Kießling re-surveyed in 2007 (Blench 2009/2011 already held by the project use the same name for the same fieldwork). Not the Central Sudanic Furu (furu1242). The statement is secondhand: Blench tabulating Kießling's unpublished field analysis.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/tone system. French expansion of the 1993 survey (Bikya pp. 36-37). p. 18: a QEL wordlist of bikyà was recorded from the last speaker in Dec 1986; p. 48 N.B.: all QELs filled in at Furu-Awa were thrown out when ISH Yaounde was dissolved in 1991. Only tone-marked name 'bikyà'.

sources.citation: Breton, Roland. 1993. Is there a Furu language group? An investigation on the Cameroon-Nigeria border. Journal of West African Languages 23(2): 97-118.
sources.note: Nothing. Bikya passage pp. 104-105 is sociolinguistic/lexicostatistic only (one full speaker left in 1986, Mrs Dana Agayando; 14% lexical similarity with Akum, 11% with Bishuo, 24% with Nsaa/Nooni; 'only an advanced morphological analysis would be able to show..'). No transcribed forms, no tone, stress or accent.
